item.title: Surprisingly Popular Voting Recovers Rankings, Surprisingly!
item.headline: Asking what others will say can improve a crowd’s answer
item.authors: Hadi Hosseini, Debmalya Mandal, Nisarg Shah, Kevin Shi
item.summary: A crowd can miss facts that a minority knows. Combining answers with predictions of others’ answers improved factual rankings in an online experiment. This journal extension of 2021 work tests four-option questions, not unrestricted truth detection.

evidence.question: Can predictions about other respondents improve factual rankings?
evidence.method: 720 MTurk participants; 60 questions about populations, box-office receipts and painting prices; six response formats.
evidence.limitations: Read the accepted author manuscript; final publisher PDF unavailable. Training/test separation is unclear in the reported averages.

explainer.finding: The format requesting both rankings and predicted rankings beat six conventional aggregation rules on ranking error across three domains.
explainer.method: The algorithm compares observed answers with predicted popularity; two conversion parameters were fitted on 15 questions.
explainer.meaning: For example, someone may know a country’s population while anticipating others’ mistaken guesses. That extra prediction can help identify overlooked knowledge.
explainer.limits: Four alternatives per question, selected tasks and an online sample limit generalization. This does not establish how to resolve political preferences.
